import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 188

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/188](https://www.erdosproblems.com/188)
- [EGMRSS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Montgomery, P. and Rothschild, B. L. and Spencer, J.
  and Straus, E. G., Euclidean {R}amsey theorems. {II}. (1975), 529--557.
- [Ts17] Tsaturian, Sergei, A {E}uclidean {R}amsey result in the plane. Electron. J. Combin. (2017),
  Paper No. 4.35, 9.
-/

namespace Erdos188

/--
The set of numbers $k$ such that $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be red/blue coloured with no pair of red
points unit distance apart, and no $k$-term arithmetic progression of blue points with distance 1.
-/
def s := { k : ℕ | ∃ blue : Set ℂ,
  (Set.univ \ blue).Pairwise (fun c₁ c₂ => dist c₁ c₂ ≠ 1) ∧
    ¬ (∃ᵉ (bs ⊆ blue) (z) (d), ‖d‖ = 1 ∧ bs.IsAPOfLengthWith k z d) }

/--
What is the smallest $k$ such that $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be red/blue coloured with no pair of red
points unit distance apart, and no $k$-term arithmetic progression of blue points with distance 1?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_188 : IsLeast s answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory by Erdős & Graham (Page 14, 15):

It has been shown that there is a large $M$ so that it is possible to partition $\mathbb{E}^2$ into
two sets $A$ and $B$ so that $A$ contains no pair of points with distance 1 and $B$ contains no A.P.
of length $M$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_188.variants.nonempty : s.Nonempty := by
  sorry

/--
Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory by Erdős & Graham (Page 15):

How small can $M$ be made? The only estimate currently known is that $M \le 10000000$ (more or less).
In the other direction, it has just been shown by R. Juhász [Ju (79)] that we must have $M \ge 5$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_188.variants.estimate : (∀ k, k ∈ s → 5 ≤ k) ∧ (∃ k ∈ s, k ≤ 10000000) := by
  sorry

end Erdos188

findings.description: The docstring says that B contains no arithmetic progression of length M, without restricting its common distance. In Lean, `s.Nonempty` only excludes progressions whose step satisfies `‖d‖ = 1`. The quotation accurately reproduces the book, but its unrestricted reading is a stronger, false assertion. The Lean statement follows the corrected interpretation endorsed by the problem page; the docstring does not explain that correction.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1980), pp. 14–15, contains the quoted unrestricted wording. https://www.erdosproblems.com/188 explicitly explains that without the unit-distance restriction no such k exists, by Alon's van der Waerden argument, and says Erdős and Graham most likely intended unit spacing.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the historical quotation but append an explicit clarification that this variant concerns blue arithmetic progressions with common distance 1, following the corrected interpretation on erdosproblems.com. Explain that the unrestricted reading is false. No change to the Lean statement is needed.

reformulations.difference: The source uses the Euclidean plane and k collinear unit-spaced blue points. Lean uses ℂ and an auxiliary set satisfying `Set.IsAPOfLengthWith`, including an explicit extended-cardinality condition, and permits k : ℕ without a positivity hypothesis.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The standard real-linear isometry ℂ ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2) preserves distances and arithmetic progressions. A step of norm 1 is nonzero, so n ↦ z + n • d is injective and the first k terms have exactly k elements; the cardinality condition adds no restriction. At k = 0 the empty progression is contained in every blue set, so 0 is automatically excluded. Scratch proofs establish both the direct Euclidean-plane equivalence and equality with the set of positive admissible lengths.

reformulations.difference: Instead of bounding the smallest admissible length directly, Lean combines a lower bound on every member of s with the existence of one member at most 10,000,000.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The upper-bound conjunct makes s nonempty, so it has a least natural-number member m. The universal lower bound implies 5 ≤ m, and minimality puts m below the upper-bound witness. Conversely, a least member with 5 ≤ m ≤ 10,000,000 supplies the upper-bound witness and bounds every member below by 5. The full equivalence with `∃ m, IsLeast s m ∧ 5 ≤ m ∧ m ≤ 10000000` was proved in Lean.

review.notes: All four declarations were checked. The main problem remains OPEN on the cited page. Tsaturian's stronger lower bound 6 does not invalidate the explicitly historical bound 5. The source qualifies the upper bound as 'more or less' and supplies no proof; the file records that historical assertion. Scratch proofs in /workspace/review/scratch.lean also exclude lengths 0, 1, and 2, rule out constant-color witnesses, and establish upward closure of s and equivalence of nonemptiness with arbitrarily large admissible lengths. Compilation completed without errors, warnings, or sorryAx dependencies in these proofs. No repository files were edited.
